body:
What is an artificial satellite?

An artificial satellite is a human-made object placed in orbit around the Earth or another celestial body. An orbit is the curved path followed by an object under the influence of gravity. A satellite remains in orbit because its forward motion and Earth's gravitational attraction together produce continuous motion around the Earth.

Artificial satellites are used for communication, observing the Earth, monitoring weather, navigation and scientific investigations. This lesson concentrates on communication, Earth-observation and meteorological satellites.

Satellite classification by purpose: A communication satellite relays signals between locations; an Earth-observation satellite gathers information about the Earth's surface or atmosphere; and a meteorological satellite observes atmospheric and related conditions for weather analysis and forecasting.

Three important functional categories

Communication satellites

Communication satellites receive radio-frequency signals transmitted from the Earth and relay them towards receiving stations or users. They support television broadcasting, telecommunications, satellite internet connections and educational communication. Their primary purpose is to transfer information rather than independently measure conditions on the Earth's surface.

Earth-observation satellites

Earth-observation satellites carry instruments that measure radiation reflected or emitted by the Earth. These measurements help identify vegetation, water bodies, land use, ocean conditions and changes occurring over time. The information is converted into images, maps and other useful data products.

Meteorological satellites

Meteorological, or weather, satellites observe clouds, atmospheric moisture, temperatures and other weather-related conditions. Their observations help meteorologists monitor storms, study atmospheric systems and prepare forecasts and warnings.

Meteorological satellites are a specialised category of Earth-observation satellites. These functional categories are not completely separate: one satellite may carry instruments for more than one application. India's INSAT programme provides important examples of multipurpose satellites.

Basic components of a satellite system

A satellite service generally involves a spacecraft, equipment on the ground and a means of transferring information between them.

  • Payload: The equipment performing the mission's main task, such as a communication transponder, camera, radar or weather-observation instrument.
  • Satellite platform: The supporting spacecraft systems that provide power, maintain suitable orientation and support satellite operation.
  • Ground segment: Ground stations and associated facilities that communicate with satellites, receive information and process or distribute it.

Even an imaging satellite sends its observations to Earth through radio communication. However, transmitting collected data does not make communication its primary mission.

How orbital position affects satellite applications

Satellites can be placed in different orbits according to the coverage and observation frequency needed. Two important orbital arrangements are geostationary and near-polar Sun-synchronous orbits.

FeatureGeostationary orbitNear-polar Sun-synchronous orbit
PositionCircular orbit above Earth's equatorLow-altitude orbit passing near the polar regions
AltitudeApproximately 35,786 kmUsually several hundred kilometres
Appearance from EarthAppears fixed above one longitudeMoves across successive ground tracks
Observation patternContinuous view of a large regionRepeated observations of different regions
Common applicationsCommunication and continuous weather monitoringResource mapping and detailed Earth observation

Why a geostationary satellite appears stationary

A geostationary satellite moves eastward in a circular orbit over the equator. Its orbital period matches Earth's rotation period, so it appears to remain above the same point on the equator. This makes it suitable for continuously serving a particular region.

The term geosynchronous is broader. A geosynchronous satellite has an orbital period matching Earth's rotation, but its orbit need not be circular and equatorial. Consequently, it need not appear stationary. Every geostationary orbit is geosynchronous, but not every geosynchronous orbit is geostationary.

Why Sun-synchronous orbits help Earth observation

A Sun-synchronous satellite passes over a given region at approximately the same local solar time on successive visits. This provides relatively consistent illumination for comparing images. As the Earth rotates beneath the satellite, successive orbital paths cover different geographical areas.

These arrangements are common, not compulsory. Communication satellites can operate in low Earth orbit, and meteorological observations can come from both geostationary and polar-orbiting satellites.

Prelims focus

  • A geostationary satellite appears fixed above a point on Earth's equator.
  • Geostationary orbital altitude is approximately 35,786 km above Earth's surface.
  • Sun-synchronous satellites revisit regions at approximately the same local solar time.
  • Meteorological satellites are a specialised form of Earth-observation satellite.
  • Trap: Satellite purpose and satellite orbit are different classifications; all weather satellites are not geostationary.

[References: NCERT, Practical Work in Geography, Class 11, Chapter 7, Introduction to Remote Sensing, printed pp. 84-90, especially Box 7.1 on p. 89; ISRO, Communication Satellites and Earth Observation Satellites, consulted 4 November 2026.]

title: Artificial Satellites: Meaning, Classification and Orbits

body:
How communication satellites transfer information

A communication satellite acts as a relay station in space. It receives radio signals sent from one location and retransmits them towards another location or a wider geographical area.

Radio signals are electromagnetic waves. They can carry television programmes, voice communication, digital information and other messages.

Uplink, transponder and downlink

Communication through a conventional satellite relay involves three main stages.

  1. Uplink: An Earth station transmits information towards the satellite.
  2. Transponder: Equipment aboard the satellite receives the signal, processes or amplifies it as required, and retransmits it. Conventional transponders often use a different frequency for transmission to reduce interference between received and transmitted signals.
  3. Downlink: The satellite transmits the signal towards a receiving station, satellite dish or other suitable terminal.

For example, a television broadcasting station can transmit a programme to a satellite, which then distributes the signal to receiving dishes located across a large geographical region.

Major applications

Television and radio broadcasting

Satellite broadcasting permits a single transmitting organisation to distribute programmes over a large coverage area. In Direct-to-Home (DTH) television, a receiving dish obtains programmes transmitted through a satellite without requiring a conventional terrestrial cable television connection.

Telecommunication and data connectivity

Communication satellites can connect distant locations through satellite terminals and ground networks. They can provide communication links to remote settlements, islands, ships and locations where terrestrial infrastructure is difficult or costly to establish.

A Very Small Aperture Terminal (VSAT) is a relatively small satellite communication earth terminal. VSAT networks are used for data connectivity and other communication services. Depending on the service, communication may be one-way or two-way.

Most ordinary mobile telephone calls and internet connections use terrestrial mobile towers, fibre-optic networks and other ground infrastructure. Satellite links may form part of certain networks, but it is incorrect to assume that every mobile call travels through a satellite.

Education, healthcare and public services

Satellite communication can support the delivery of lessons, training, information and specialist consultations to geographically separated institutions.

  • Tele-education: Educational content is transmitted to distant classrooms; suitably equipped systems can also support interaction.
  • Telemedicine: Communication links connect healthcare facilities with remote medical specialists.
  • Public information: Broadcasting networks distribute educational, agricultural and awareness programmes over wide areas.

Communication during disasters

Earthquakes, cyclones and floods can damage terrestrial communication networks. Satellite communication may provide an alternative connection for emergency coordination when suitable terminals, power supplies and operational satellite services are available.

Satellite communication does not itself detect a cyclone. It carries information, including warnings and emergency messages, between the relevant organisations and users.

Why geostationary satellites are widely used

A geostationary satellite remains in approximately the same direction when viewed from a fixed location on Earth. A ground dish can therefore maintain its orientation towards that satellite without continuously tracking a rapidly moving object.

Its high altitude also allows coverage of a large geographical region. However, radio signals must travel considerable distances, producing greater communication delay than shorter links. Geostationary coverage is also less suitable for extreme polar regions.

These advantages and limitations explain why geostationary systems are important for regional communication, while some modern communication networks use constellations of satellites in low Earth orbit.

India's communication satellite programmes

Indian National Satellite System

The Indian National Satellite System (INSAT) is a major Indian satellite programme supporting telecommunications, broadcasting, meteorological observation and other public services.

The INSAT system was established in 1983 with the commissioning of INSAT-1B. It became an important part of India's communication infrastructure and helped expand television and other services.

GSAT communication satellites

The GSAT series includes Indian communication satellites used for services such as broadcasting and telecommunications. The INSAT and GSAT names identify Indian satellite programmes or mission families; they should not be treated as names for entirely different physical principles of communication.

EDUSAT: a dedicated educational satellite

EDUSAT, also called GSAT-3, was launched on 20 September 2004. It was India's first satellite dedicated specifically to educational services and supported satellite-based classroom communication.

EDUSAT is an important historical example of a communication satellite designed around a particular educational requirement. It should not be confused with the broader INSAT system or treated as a currently operating satellite.

Communication satellite: Relays information between users or stations.
Earth-observation satellite: Measures physical conditions and features of the Earth.
Weather satellite: Measures atmospheric and related conditions; its observations can subsequently be communicated to users through different networks.

Prelims focus

  • Uplink means transmission from Earth towards a satellite.
  • Downlink means transmission from a satellite towards Earth.
  • A transponder receives and relays communication signals.
  • The INSAT system was established in 1983 with the commissioning of INSAT-1B.
  • EDUSAT or GSAT-3 was launched on 20 September 2004 as India's first dedicated educational satellite.
  • Trap: DTH broadcasting is satellite communication, not an Earth-surface imaging service.

[References: NCERT, Fundamentals of Human Geography, Class 12, Chapter 8, Transport and Communication, printed p. 79; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, Chapter 10, Transport and Communication, printed pp. 122-123; ISRO, Communication Satellites and Satellite Communication and Lease of Transponders; ISRO, EDUSAT mission page, consulted 4 November 2026.]

body:
What is remote sensing?

Remote sensing means obtaining information about an object or area without placing the measuring instrument in direct physical contact with it. Satellite remote sensing uses instruments aboard orbiting spacecraft to observe the Earth's surface, oceans and atmosphere.

Different materials interact differently with electromagnetic radiation. Water, vegetation, exposed soil and built-up areas may reflect, absorb or emit different amounts of radiation at different wavelengths. Sensors measure these differences to obtain information about the observed region.

Satellite observations can cover large and difficult-to-reach areas repeatedly. They are particularly useful for studying changes in vegetation, flood extent, land use, coastal conditions and natural resources.

Passive and active remote sensing

Passive remote sensing

A passive sensor measures radiation that originates naturally. Optical sensors commonly measure sunlight reflected by the Earth's surface. Thermal infrared sensors measure radiation emitted by surfaces or atmospheric substances because of their temperature.

Consequently, visible-light imaging of the surface depends on sunlight and is generally unsuitable for ordinary night-time imaging. Thermal infrared observations can also be made at night because they do not require reflected sunlight.

Clouds can obstruct an optical sensor's view of the land. This makes optical observations difficult during extensive monsoon cloud cover.

Active remote sensing

An active sensor sends out its own signal and measures the signal returned from an observed surface.

Radar satellites transmit microwave signals and measure the returned energy. Many satellite imaging radars can obtain useful observations during both day and night and through ordinary cloud cover. This makes radar particularly valuable for monitoring floods or agricultural land during cloudy weather.

The ability to penetrate clouds does not mean that every radar observation is unaffected by weather, vegetation or surface conditions. The recorded signal still depends on the target and the properties of the transmitted radiation.

Understanding satellite images

Pixels and spatial resolution

A digital satellite image consists of small picture elements called pixels. Each pixel contains a recorded value representing the sensor's measurement for a particular ground area.

Spatial resolution refers to the ability to distinguish small or closely spaced ground features. In general, a sensor with finer spatial resolution can distinguish smaller details, although the amount of information also depends on image quality and other characteristics.

Spectral information

Spectral resolution concerns a sensor's ability to record information in different wavelength ranges or bands. Multispectral sensors observe a scene in several bands, allowing information to be obtained that may not be apparent in an ordinary visible-light picture.

Healthy green vegetation strongly reflects near-infrared radiation. This property helps distinguish vegetation from many other surfaces and supports crop-condition and vegetation-cover studies.

In a commonly used standard false-colour composite, near-infrared measurements are displayed as red. Healthy vegetation may therefore appear bright red rather than its natural green colour. Such an image is not necessarily an incorrectly processed photograph; it intentionally uses artificial display colours to reveal useful information.

Temporal resolution and repeated observations

Temporal resolution describes how frequently a satellite system can observe the same area. Repeated observations allow changes to be detected over time, such as expanding cities, seasonal crop growth or floodwater recession.

A satellite passing over the same region does not necessarily obtain an equally useful cloud-free image on every visit. Observation frequency and usable observation frequency can therefore differ.

From satellite measurement to useful information

Remote sensing produces measurements, which must be interpreted before they become useful for planning. A simplified process is as follows:

  1. A sensor records radiation associated with features of the Earth.
  2. The measurements are transmitted to a receiving station.
  3. The data are processed into images or other observation products.
  4. Features such as vegetation, water and built-up land are identified and mapped.
  5. The resulting information is combined with other observations and used for decisions.

A Geographic Information System (GIS) can organise and analyse spatial information from satellite observations, field surveys and other sources. Remote sensing collects observations; GIS helps combine and use geographically referenced information. They are complementary technologies, not identical concepts.

A satellite image is not automatically a complete ground-level explanation. Cloud cover, mixed land features, interpretation errors and changing conditions can affect results. Field observations and other data may be necessary to confirm the meaning of satellite measurements.

Prelims focus

  • Remote sensing obtains information without direct physical contact with the observed object.
  • Passive sensors detect naturally reflected or emitted radiation.
  • Active radar sensors transmit their own signals and measure the return.
  • Radar imaging can provide day-and-night observations through ordinary cloud cover.
  • Spatial resolution concerns detail; spectral resolution concerns wavelength bands; temporal resolution concerns observation frequency.
  • Trap: Thermal infrared observation does not require reflected sunlight, unlike ordinary visible-light imaging.

[References: NCERT, Practical Work in Geography, Class 11, Chapter 7, Introduction to Remote Sensing, printed pp. 84-99, particularly pp. 86-90 and 92-99; ISRO, RISAT-1 mission page, sections on mission and applications, consulted 4 November 2026.]
